p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t:
Meta ads have three layers: campaign, ad set and ad. Set each thing at the right layer.
For a new store, test interests with ABO, which gives each ad set a fixed budget.
Scale winners with CBO, which uses one budget for the whole campaign. Do not scale with ABO.

Sources disagree on structure and budget, so test both in your own account.
Wait for enough purchase data before you switch structures.

Test one idea at a time. Each ad set holds one interest and one message.
Choose **Purchase** as the goal for tests. Clicks and likes do not show who buys.
Use ABO (you set the money per ad set) for tests. Use CBO (one budget for the whole campaign) only after you know a winner.

Keep the account simple: a few campaigns, not dozens.
Keep winners, turn off losers, and stop tests after a short time.
Set the start to **midnight on the next day**, in the ad account's time zone, so the budget spreads over the day.

Start with the **recommended setup**. Change it only where it fails to make profit.
Do **not** connect an Instagram account to the Facebook ad.

Do not limit ads to certain hours. Facebook learns the best times in about **1-2 days**.
Wait for **"All edits saved"** before leaving an ad page, so your last change is kept.
Account hierarchy and levels
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: Meta (the company behind Facebook and Instagram) runs Ads Manager, its ad tool, with **three levels**: campaign (the goal and budget strategy),
ad set (budget, audience, placements, which are where the ad appears, and message destinations, where a click leads), and ad (identity,
which is the page or account the ad comes from; creative, which is the picture, video or text; and the ad name).
Settings must be made at the correct level, so a destination or audience change made at campaign level will not apply to the ad set.
The ad account (the account that holds all your ads) holds campaigns, campaigns hold ad sets, and ad sets hold the ads.
Each campaign has **one objective** (the goal, such as sales), and each ad set holds one audience (the people the ad is shown to).
At campaign level the **optional budget** is set.
At ad set level the countries, age, gender, interests (topics people like, used to find buyers), placements, schedule and, under ABO (Ad set Budget Optimization, a fixed budget set on each ad set),
the budget are set. At ad level the media, copy (the words around the ad), headline and destination link are set. One campaign holds many ad sets, and each ad set holds many ads.
The campaign defines the **objective** (sales, traffic or leads), the ad set holds targeting (choosing who sees the ad: countries, audiences, placements, start date and time),
and the ad combines the creative (video, image or carousel, which is a swipeable set of images) with the ad copy.
Settings are entered from the top level down, so **campaign settings** are set before the ad set and the ad.
Settings made at a higher level affect everything below it, so the structure must be **understood before building**.
In the Power Editor hierarchy (Meta's older advanced ad tool), the campaign represents the industry or theme, each ad set targets **one precise interest** (a topic a person likes, such as yoga),
and each ad holds the creative shown in the feed (the main scrolling list of posts).

in a Facebook campaign, ad sets sit inside the campaign, ads sit inside the ad sets, and the audience is chosen at the ad set level. **Name ad sets after their audience**, for example website visitors within 7 days.
Ad level hierarchy table
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: **Campaign**: The offer you want to sell (for example resistance bands) and the optimization objective (the result Meta aims for, for example Conversions,
which means sales or sign-ups)
**Ad set**: The target audience, budget, schedule, placement (where the ad shows: mobile, desktop, iPhone, iPad and so on), and bidding for clicks (how much you pay per click)
**Ad**: The creative: image, video and copy
For new Meta sales campaigns, choose the **Sales objective**.
Awareness (showing your brand to many people), traffic (clicks to a site), engagement (likes and comments), leads (sign-ups),
and app promotion (app installs) are not recommended for direct-response ad accounts that aim to make money. Direct-response means ads that aim for an immediate sale or sign-up.

Set the objective that matches the real goal, such as **conversions** (tracked actions like a sale or sign-up) for leads or sales, or catalog sales (sales from a product list, called a catalog) for product sales.
Choosing another objective, such as traffic or engagement while wanting sales, to steer who sees the ad is outdated.
Campaign objective: set **Conversions**, unless you are driving traffic for retargeting (showing ads again to people who already visited your site).
Choosing the purchase conversion objective targets audiences with high purchase intent (people likely to buy), so **CPMs are higher** than in engagement campaigns.
CPM is the cost to show your ad 1,000 times. Interest targeting determines the first sales in early testing.
Create > Choose a buying type: **Auction** (Meta bids for each ad view automatically). Keep Auction for new sales campaigns and do not switch to Reach and frequency or other manual buying types.
Campaign details: keep Buying type on Auction, keep Campaign objective on Sales, and **leave Product information untouched**, because it only makes Meta suggest products to people
and is not needed for a basic setup.
Reach and frequency campaigns use buying type Reach and Frequency and objective Reach. When asked, set **how many impressions** (views) per person per day and over how many days.
Total impressions per person = impressions per day multiplied by number of days. Example: 2 impressions per day for 7 days equals **14 impressions** in total.

Full launch procedure for a new store
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: Create a campaign with the objective Sales, choose Manual campaign setup (not Advantage+/CBO), and name it after the store.
2. Set budget optimization to **ABO** (budget set per ad set) so each interest test gets the same budget.
Confirm the Meta pixel (a small tracking code on your store that reports sales to Meta) is connected and that the pixel ID (the number that identifies your pixel,
last three digits) matches the one shown in the Shopify Facebook app (the link between your Shopify store and Facebook).
4. Set the conversion event to Purchase. 4a. Set the daily budget per ad set to **$5** and schedule the start for the next day at 6:00 a.m. (the source's own choice; 12 p.m. or 12 a.m. also work).
5. Set location to Switzerland, age minimum 25+, and leave the first ad set as Broad (no interests, a wide audience) with German as the language, because the ads are in German.
6. Leave placements on Advantage+ placements (Meta chooses where the ad appears automatically).
7. Select the correct Facebook Page and do not connect an Instagram account, so clicks go directly to the landing page (the page a visitor arrives on).
8. Use manual upload (not a catalog) with a single image or video, write primary text, headline with the offer, and description, and set the CTA (call to action, the button text).
9. Duplicate the ad set to create four ad sets with the same creative setup, each testing a different interest, then review and publish.

Budget optimization: CBO versus ABO: Definitions
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: CBO (Campaign Budget Optimization, now called Advantage campaign budget): **one budget** is set on the

campaign, and Meta distributes it across the ad sets.
ABO (Ad set Budget Optimization): a budget is set on **each ad set**, and each ad set spends its own budget.
Principle: CBO is used for **scaling** (spending more on what already works) because Meta distributes one campaign budget across the best-performing ad sets.
ABO is used for testing because it forces a fixed budget into each ad set.
Principle: **ABO keeps spending under your control** because a new pixel has no purchase data for Meta to optimize (improve the ads automatically) with.
CBO works by sending several copies of the same interest to different pockets of the audience (small groups inside the audience), so the campaign can shift budget to the pocket that performs best.
For example, a $10 daily budget at a $10 CPM reaches about **1,000 people per day**, which is a tiny share of a 30 million audience.
Under CBO, **after about a week** the campaign shifts most budget to the best interest ad set. If that ad set drops off, budget flows back to the others.

**Single product test**
Recommended structure: CBO
p.h: When each structure applies (Sources agree and differ)

p.t:
**Several different products tested at once**
Recommended structure: ABO, not as a beginner
**Beginners and mid-stage accounts**

Recommended structure: CBO as the default
**Scaling proven winners**
Recommended structure: CBO

**Testing new interests or a new store**
Recommended structure: ABO
**Creative testing with a fixed budget per creative**

Recommended structure: ABO
**Multi-interest tests on a new store, German-speaking markets**

Recommended structure: ABO with several similar interests in one ad set at $5
**Default Source E recommendation**

Recommended structure: CBO; ABO advised against
**Lead generation with Source A's campaigns**
Recommended structure: CBO on
**ABO is not a scaling method** and should not be used by beginners to scale, because it burns the budget fast. Scaling with ABO is a mistake; move winners to a CBO for scaling.
ABO only makes sense with a **large budget reserve** (money kept aside beyond the daily spend).
When each structure applies (Sources agree and differ) (continued)
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: **Use CBO only for scaling** with known winning interests and creatives (the ads themselves), because CBO would otherwise put most money on one interest and leave the rest of the test with none.
A new store that tests interests should use **ABO rather than CBO**, so that each interest receives the same fixed budget for a fair comparison. CBO is better used later when scaling winners.

To decide between CBO and ABO for your account, **run the same proven interest in both structures** for a set test period and compare ROAS (return on ad spend, money back per dollar spent) and purchases.
Keep ABO for testing new interests, and use CBO for scaling only once an interest is already profitable on ABO.
**Test both** CBO and ABO in your own account, since the better structure depends on the specific ad account.
Use ABO campaigns for creative testing, because the budget is fixed per ad set and each creative can be read on its own.

When a winner is scaled into CBO or cost-cap campaigns (a limit on what you pay per result), Meta controls the spend allocation, so put **at least two to three creatives** in each ad set to keep delivery from
concentrating on a single ad.
In a separate ABO test campaign the budget is set at ad set level, so **every creative gets spend** regardless of early results.
In a scaling CBO, some new creatives may get little or no spend, so you cannot tell whether they work.
Running an ABO scaling ad set alongside a separate testing ad set that targets the same interest **usually makes the testing sets lose delivery** (stop being shown).
**Stay on CBO while testing**, because ABO means funding every ad set manually, which takes a large budget. Let the algorithm allocate spend, and add bid or cost caps later once the pixel has data.
**Switch to ABO only after** the pixel has real purchase data.
Switch from CBO to ABO only after around **80-100 website purchases** from the CBO, with rich data (a large amount of detail from your ads) from custom ads and high-intensity testing.
Move from ABO to CBO or other campaign types **only after** the pixel has collected good purchase data, because Meta can then identify likely buyers and allocate spend itself.
Use ABO only when testing **several different products** at once, and not as a beginner, because ABO uses up the budget quickly. Use CBO for a single product test and for scaling.

Lifetime budget optimization (a budget for the whole run of a campaign, not per day) is **hardly ever recommended**. It has specific uses, such as some Black Friday setups, and is only used in those cases.
Conflicting position on the test budget structure
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: Source D and other sources recommend a **CBO test** (Sales objective, CBO, highest volume) as the standard test structure.
Source C recommends **ABO for testing** and says CBO was unreliable for one product: CBO broke even (made no profit) or lost money, so ad set budgets were used instead.
Source C's Advantage+ campaign note (Advantage+ is Meta's automated campaign type): Advantage+ campaigns are scaled with the **same strategy** used for other campaigns.
Testing a CBO that holds only one winning creative limits ad delivery; add **two to three creatives** even when one ad keeps producing sales.
Starting point: a profitable ad with a **ROAS of roughly 2 to 3**, and a testing-phase CPA (cost per acquisition,

what one sale costs you) of about 10 to 50 dollars.
Step 1: the ad was duplicated into a CBO with three ads and a **$200 budget**, and CPA rose with almost no sales.

Step 2: a second CBO with a **$20 budget** and the same ads also failed.
Step 3: the ad in a separate testing campaign with a **$5 budget** performed well.
Result: CBO was unreliable for this product because Facebook shifts budget between ads and removing weaker ads disrupted delivery, so **ABO was used instead**.
The seller used campaign budget optimization (CBO) on Facebook instead of ad set budgets (ABO).
p.h: Case: budget flow in a seller's CBO

p.t: **Most of the spend** flowed to the broad interest and online-shopper audiences.
Budgets set per ad set make a profitable ad set **stop at its daily cap** (the most it may spend per day)
while break-even ad sets keep spending. This forces constant manual reallocation (moving money by hand), so use CBO in campaigns that need it.
With ABO, a budget set per ad set is fixed, for example 25 dollars for each of four ad sets.
Meta offers a setting that lets it move part of an ad set budget to other ad sets, which undermines manual control, so **ABO is not recommended**.
CBO settings and budget figures: Setting Procedure
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: Set **one total daily budget** across all targeting groups (the groups of people you target)
and let Facebook automatically allocate spending to the most profitable audiences and placements; for example,
allocate $100/day and Facebook distributes where it performs best.
Campaign level: **turn on Advantage+ campaign budget** (CBO), enter the test budget there, since Meta then distributes that single campaign budget across the ad sets.
Budget > Budget strategy: choose Advantage+ campaign budget (CBO). Enter the daily amount in **Daily budget in USD**. Choosing CBO removes the ad set budget suggestions shown in Ads Manager.
The CBO toggle (the on/off switch) is off by default in the lead generation setup and **must be turned on**.

Ad set > Budget: check that the budget shown is the campaign budget, because an ad set still set to ABO will show its own budget. If so, go back and **change it to Campaign budget optimization** before continuing.
The Advantage+ sales campaign toggle is shown as on in the recommended setup for new sales campaigns, and the campaign-level budget is used.
If an ad set shows that Advantage+ is off for Budget, that ad set is not using the campaign budget and **should be checked before publishing**.
Campaign level CBO test: choose the Sales objective, switch Campaign budget to Advantage+ campaign budget, and set the daily budget to a test amount.
**Use $50** for a normal test, with $75 or $100 for a more aggressive test; more spend yields data faster and bad campaigns can be cut earlier.

CBO campaign-level settings: turn off the Advantage+ sales campaign recommendations, leave Campaign bid strategy at its default, and set the Performance goal (the result Meta aims for) to **Maximize**
**number of conversions**. Use Conversion event purchase (the tracked action) and confirm the correct pixel dataset (the stored data from your pixel) is selected.
Set the campaign to CBO and **allow Meta to share the budget** across the ad sets in the testing campaigns. This lets Meta move spend toward the ad sets that perform best.
Signals Meta reads under CBO
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: Meta's Advantage campaign budget (CBO) **reads signals** (numbers Meta checks) such as CTR (the share of viewers who click), CPA,
CPC (cost per click), conversion volume and ROAS. It moves budget toward ads converting at lower cost and reduces budget for underperformers **throughout each day**.
Spend is therefore treated as Meta's confidence signal for each ad.
With CBO turned on, Meta spreads the campaign budget across the ad sets to find more results. This makes the single campaign budget **the one control** you set for the test.
With a daily budget of 500 USD, Ads Manager shows an average spend of about 500 USD per day,
a maximum daily spend of 875 USD (175 percent of the daily budget) and a **maximum weekly spend of 3,500 USD** (seven times the daily budget).
Meta can spend more on some days and less on others, but it stays within the weekly cap.
With an Advantage campaign budget, the maximum weekly spend equals **seven times the daily budget**.
Daily spend can vary above or below the average within the week, but the weekly total cannot exceed the cap.
The example shows a maximum daily spend of $43.75 and a maximum weekly spend of $175, which matches a $25 daily budget.
Facebook has no minimum budget, and a daily budget of **$1** is enough to keep a campaign active. Keep it running at this level until you have money to scale it back up.

Lifetime and ad set spending limits
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: Ad set > Ad set spending limits: tick the box and enter a daily minimum or a daily maximum for the ad set.
**Use this only when** a specific spend limit is needed.
Meta's existing customer budget cap (an older Meta limit on spend) **can no longer be applied to new campaigns**.
To get a similar effect, use Campaign budget optimization together with ad set spending limits, and campaigns that already use the cap keep working.
Testing Architecture
**Start** a test on Meta with one ABO campaign. ABO means you set the budget on each ad set.

Use 6 to 10 ad sets in that campaign.
Each ad set targets a single interest, which is one topic people like, such as a hobby.

Spend **$10 to $15 per day** on each ad set.
Each ad set runs 3 to 5 different creatives. A creative is one ad: a picture or a video.

Testing campaign structure: an ABO campaign with **7 to 8** ad sets, each targeting one single interest.
Start each of those ad sets at about **$15** budget.

Put three ads with different creatives inside each ad set.
Testing structure: one ABO campaign with **five** ad sets.
Each ad set targets exactly one interest.

Each ad set has at least three creatives (image or video).
That makes **15 ads** in total.

Test **three CBO campaigns**. CBO means one budget for the whole campaign, and Meta splits it across the ad sets.
Set each CBO to the amount you are willing to spend.

When one CBO wins, **increase its budget** to reach more people from the same audience.
Launch **three CBOs** with the same budget and targeting.

Put four ad sets in each CBO, with identical settings.
After a few days, keep the one or two CBOs that perform.
Turn off the rest.
Testing Structures (continued)
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t:
Launch the same ads in **two separate CBO campaigns**.
Turn on budget sharing so Meta can move money between ad sets.
Give each ad set one main concept.

Add 3 to 5 variations per ad set. Vary the hook (the first seconds that grab attention), the script or the angle (the reason or emotion behind the ad).
**Start with a $75 budget.**
Scale the budget fast in steps: $150, $300, $500, $750 and $1,000. Go higher if the results hold.
The goal of this phase is to find the winning creatives and angles.
Testing setup for two CBO testing lanes: a **Main CBO** prepared for bid cap stays unpublished. A bid cap is a maximum price you accept per purchase.

**CBO 1** is for Kalo rips. A rip is a copy of a winning ad that is re-cut.
**CBO 2** is for custom ads.
Testing lane: an ABO testing campaign on cost cap with tROAS or tCPA.
A cost cap limits the price per result. tROAS (target return on ad spend) and tCPA (target cost per action) are price goals for the algorithm.

Use **one ad set per creative batch**.
Per creative, write **3** primary texts, **3** headlines and **1** description.

Set up the main CBO plus **one** testing CBO.
Put one concept in each ad set.
Put 3 to 5 creatives in each ad set.

The base Meta testing unit is one ad set.
That ad set holds one concept with 3 to 5 creatives.
All of it sits inside one CBO.
For English-speaking markets (US, Australia, New Zealand and Canada), **one interest** per ad set at $5 worked better.

For German-speaking markets, several similar interests in one ad set at $5 worked better.
Choose the test structure per country. Do not use one template everywhere.
Testing Principles
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t:
A CBO with only **one** winning creative limits ad delivery (how many people the ad reaches).
Add **two to three** creatives, even if one ad keeps making sales.

More creatives give Facebook more options and usually improve overall results.
Use **ABO** for testing. It controls how much budget each interest gets.
Use **CBO** only for scaling, with interests and creatives you already know win.

Facebook prefers the older creative, the one with more engagement (likes, comments, shares) and sales data.
A new creative next to a proven winner gets little spend.

So **always split** them into separate ad sets.
Use a **separate ad set** for each new creative test.

Keep the winning ad set as a control (a fixed reference you compare against).
Then spend follows the new creative results, not the old winner.

For multi-product tests with ABO: all products in the same campaign and pixel should be in the same category.
A pixel is the tracking code that records sales from your store.

Example: all construction books, not a mix of nursing and plumbing.
Mixing categories under one pixel makes the test harder to read.

Meta's algorithm (the system that picks who sees the ad) can still handle the mix.
Testing campaigns are meant to run for a **short window**.
Testing both structures in your own account, with **automatic rules** running overnight. Automatic rules are settings that act on their own, so no manual checks are needed.

Source A's Sandbox campaign uses **2 ads** per test: 1 control and 1 variation.
This split-tests creatives without affecting your core campaigns.

Mistake: using a **single creative** inside a CBO test limits delivery.
Power Five framework: **start with the recommendations**. Change things only where they fail to produce profit.
Multi-Product ABO Setup
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: 1. Create **one campaign** with Campaign budget off (Advantage+ campaign budget off). Advantage+ is Meta's automatic setup.

Set the budget at ad set level.
2. Set the Budget strategy to **Ad set budget**.
3. Leave Ad set budget sharing and Advantage+ options at default, unless a test needs changes.

4. A common starting budget is **$50 per ad set** for one product with three creatives.
5. The money is divided per creative: $50 divided by 3 creatives.
6. Products can start at **$25, $50 or $100**, depending on how hard you test each product.
When budget sharing is on, Meta can move up to **20%** of an ad set's budget to other ad sets in the same campaign.

Meta does this when it likely improves results.
To keep the budget strictly in each ad set for testing, **turn it off**.

Conflicting setting: Source D' CBO testing structure turns budget sharing on. Its ABO test turns it off for strict testing.
Use budget sharing **on** for CBO tests.
Use it **off** for strict ABO tests.
Stay on **CBO** while scaling with concepts you know win.

The Main CBO holds **only proven concepts**, with stable spend. Winners are folded back in.
Scale proven concepts in the main CBO.

Test ripped winners in CBO 2.
Advantage+ campaigns are scaled the same way as other campaigns.
They use a single ad set.

When old creatives die out (stop working), **add new creatives**.
Scaling with ABO is a **mistake**.
Move winners to a CBO for scaling.

Use CBO for scaling only with known winning interests and creatives.
Otherwise CBO puts spend on one interest and starves the rest of the test.
Once an interest is already profitable on ABO, **move it to CBO** to scale.

When a winner is scaled into CBO or cost-cap campaigns, Meta controls how the spend is split.
Test with Meta's **recommended budget** first. Then scale.
Campaign counts and account structure
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t:
Meta prefers a simple account with about **2 to 5 campaigns**.
The practical setup here is **1 campaign, 1 ad set and 1 ad**.

Avoid many complicated ad structures.
Use a simple account with a few campaigns and very broad targeting.

Do not build dozens or hundreds of hyper-segmented ad sets (ad sets cut into tiny audience slices).
Let the pixel find the buyers from its data.
Hyper-stacked targeting stacks many filters: interest, online-shopper behavior, household income above $100,000, cities, gender, age brackets and single placements.

This produced huge numbers of ad sets.
It needed about **50 hours per week** from three people.
Use **one CBO** with one broad campaign.

Do not test different interests in it.
Do not add multiple account strategies.
Conflicting guidance: Source C's new-store procedure tests several interests in ABO ad sets inside one campaign. This goes against the one-campaign rule.

For a **mature account** with proven broad targeting, follow the one-CBO rule.
For a **new store** that must compare interests, run the ABO interest tests.
Power Five framework has five parts: auto advanced matching (Meta matches customer details to find buyers), a simple account with few broad campaigns, campaign budget optimization,

automatic placements, and dynamic ads for remarketing (showing ads again to people who already visited).
Apply **all five first**.
Then change only the parts that fail to produce profit.

Recommended setup: a **main CBO** prepared for bid cap that stays unpublished.
Add **CBO 1** for Kalo rips and **CBO 2** for custom ads.
Each extra CBO splits the data further.
Running two or more testing CBOs causes **cannibalisation** (your own campaigns compete with each other) in the short term.

This raises CPC (cost per click) and CPM (cost per 1,000 views).
It is still the fastest route to a winning creative.
Testing campaign counts (continued)
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t:
Running several CBOs at once means your campaigns compete in the same auctions. CPC and CPM go up.
Accept this as a **short-term cost** for finding winners faster.

Testing campaigns are meant to run for a short window.
Run **at most two** testing CBOs in parallel.

More than **three** CBOs in total fragments the data across the account.
Keep the number of CBOs low. Start with the main CBO and CBO 2.

Open CBO 3 only when budget allows.
Never run **four or five** CBOs. That fragments the data.
Testing campaign for two separate CBOs: the same ads launched in two separate CBO campaigns.

**Main CBO**
Purpose: Scale proven concepts

Contents: Only proven concepts, stable spend, winners folded back in
**CBO 2 (Kalodata rips)**
Purpose: Test ripped winners

Contents: Kalodata winners (Kalodata is a product research tool), ripped and re-cut, 3-5 creatives per concept
**CBO 3 (custom ads)**
Purpose: Test new messaging
Contents: VSLs (video sales letters) or statics (still images) built from your research: new pain point, avatar (your made-up picture of a buyer), or messaging
A typical CBO test ad set holds **3 creatives**.
p.h: Ad sets per campaign, creatives per ad set and concepts: Ad sets and creative counts

p.t:
The first round of a product test uses about **9 creatives** in total across ad sets.
Add creatives by **duplicating the ad set**.

A test with 4 products is repeated for each product.
Maximum **20 to 25 ads** per Facebook ad set.

When you add new creatives to an existing ad set, do not go above **20 ads** total.
Add at least **two to three creatives** to each ad set in a CBO.
This keeps delivery from concentrating on one ad.
Ad set naming and duplication for CBO test
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: 1. Create **one CBO campaign** with one ad set and three creatives.

2. Name the first ad set **AdSet 1** for reference.
3. Duplicate the ad set as **AdSet 2**. Rename the ads **B1 to B6**, testing the first six creatives.
4. On day 3, continue the same method with the next creatives. You get **nine creatives** in the first round (B1 to B9).
5. Keep the same CBO. Duplicate it for each further batch: AdSet 4, AdSet 5, AdSet 6, AdSet 7.

1. Tick the first ad set and click **Duplicate**, choosing **four copies**.
2. In each copy, change **only the audience**.

3. Open Suggestions, pick **one new related interest**, and remove the previous interest so only one remains.
4. Rename the ad set to match the new interest.
5. Leave the ads and all other settings as they are. The duplicate already carries them.

One ad set holds **one concept**. A concept is defined by one avatar and one angle.
Put **3 to 5 creatives** inside it.
Never mix different concepts in one ad set. You will not know which message did the work.

The base Meta testing unit is one ad set holding one concept with 3-5 creatives, all inside one CBO.
Never mix two concepts inside one ad set.

Then you cannot tell which message caused the result.
A concept can be a specific pain point or promise.
It can be a distinct messaging angle.

It can be a demographic cut: ethnicity, age group or life stage.
It can be an avatar with different objections.

Variations of the same message share **one ad set**.
A new message gets **its own ad set**.

In the ABO testing lane, per creative: **3** primary texts (the main body text of the ad), **3** headlines and **1** description.
Tests with two CBOs: **one concept** per ad set.

Put 3-5 creatives in each ad set.
Creative tests use **3 to 4 ads** per dynamic campaign (campaigns where Meta mixes ad parts automatically).

Use **3 to 4 unique ads** per promotion.
These numbers come from the campaign type table.
Ad Set Creation
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t:
1. Name the ad set: **date first**, then audience, then country, then placement.
2. Under Conversion, choose **Website**.

3. Performance goal: **Maximize number of conversions**.
4. Pixel: select the pixel connected to your Shopify store. Shopify is the online store software.

5. Conversion event: **Purchase**.
6. If Meta shows a warning about choosing another conversion event, and your Purchase tracking is set up correctly, **ignore it** and continue.
7. Turn **off** Dynamic creative for the testing phase. Dynamic creative is Meta's automatic mix of ad parts.

8. Budget and schedule: set the daily budget for the ad set from the price tier.
9. Start date: **the next day, at midnight**.
10. Locations: click **Edit** and target the top four or five countries. Example: United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and United Kingdom.

11. Advantage+ audience: click **Switch to original audience**.
12. Age: **18 to 65+**.
13. Gender: select **all**, unless the product is for one gender only.

14. Detailed targeting: add **one interest only**.
15. Placements: choose **Advantage+ placement**. Placement means where the ad shows, such as Feed or Stories.

1. Name the ad after its video or its angle. Example: Video 1 if nothing better fits.
2. Select the **Facebook Page** that represents the brand.

3. If the store has its own Instagram account, use it too.
4. Otherwise, a Facebook Page can also show ads on Instagram.

5. Click **Create ad**, then **Manual upload**, then **Single image or video**.
6. Under Ad media, click **Add video** and upload the file from your computer.

7. Trimming is optional.
8. Check that the dimensions are shown as fine.
9. Click **Next**, then **Done**.

10. Fill in primary text, headline, description and the call to action button (CTA, the button such as Shop now).
11. Destination: **paste the product page URL**.
12. Set up the URL parameters (extra tags added to the link so you can track it) in the Tracking section.
Advantage+ campaign creation
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t:
1. **Duplicate the campaign**.
2. When asked, choose **Advantage+** instead of manual settings.

3. The result is **one ad set** containing several ads.
4. The budget is set on that ad set.
Campaign bid strategy: start with **Highest volume or value**.
Other options are Cost per result goal, ROAS goal and Bid cap.

Use those other options only once you know why you need them. They change how Meta bids in auctions.
Set the campaign bid strategy to **highest volume**.
CBO campaign level: leave Campaign bid strategy at its **default**.
Ad set > Conversion > Performance goal: use **Maximize number of conversions** for nearly all accounts.

Maximize value conversions is only for specific cases.
The other options in the dropdown are not used for standard sales campaigns.

Performance goal: **Maximize number of conversions**.
Testing lane: ABO testing campaign on cost cap with tROAS or tCPA.
Bidding to clicks at ad set level while the campaign has **fewer than 30 conversions**.

Optimizing an ad set for Conversions only makes sense after it has about **30 conversions**.
Below that, Facebook does not have enough data.

So optimize for **clicks** instead.
Value rules let Meta value different audiences differently.
Value rules are complex and not needed for standard setups.
So **leave them disabled**.
Conversion event and conversion location
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: Ad set > Conversion > Conversion location: choose **Website**.

The old Website and shop option no longer exists.
So traffic from ads goes to the website, where checkout happens.
Use **Website** as the conversion location and **Purchase** as the objective.

Other objectives such as engagement, traffic or link clicks bring cheap visitors who rarely buy.
That gives weak data.

Ad set > Conversion > Conversion event: select **Purchase** every time for sales campaigns.
Ad set conversion event: set to **Purchase**.

Make sure the conversion location is **website**.
Pick **your own pixel**.
Set the conversion event to **Purchase**.

Optimizing for Add to Cart, Initiate Checkout or Traffic makes many of those events.
But those attract lower-intent users, so few buy.

For testing, **always choose Purchase** as the conversion event.
A purchase goal gives **fewer events** than add to cart.
But the events are more useful for a dropshipping business (selling products shipped by a supplier).
If Meta warns you to choose another conversion event, and your Purchase event is set up correctly, **the warning can be ignored**.

Confirm the correct pixel dataset is selected at campaign level.
Select the **new pixel** for the ad set.
Ad set audience: choose the **top 4 countries** by sales.
p.h: Ad set audience and targeting: Locations and Age

p.t:
Example: only the United States, if the product ships only there.
Set the age range **wide**.
Leave Advantage+ audience **on**.

Target **ePacket or T5** countries: US, UK, CAN, AU, NZ. ePacket and T5 are fast, trackable shipping services.
Usually the age range **begins at 21**.

Age normally **21 and above**.
Locations: United States, United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and Canada.

Locations: United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and United Kingdom.
Age: **18 to 65+**.
Gender: select **all**, unless the product is for one gender only.
Test location example: Switzerland, age **25+**, with German as the language, because the ads are in German.
Interests and audience structure
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t:
Use **one interest only** per ad set.
Each ad set targets **exactly one interest**.

Leave the audience settings **broad**.
Leave the first ad set as **Broad** (no interests), with German as the language.

Interests versus broad: Source A's practice is simple, very broad targeting.
Source C's tests use one interest per ad set.
Example: an ad set with three ads, so the platform compares three creatives against the same audience.
Testing several creatives in one ad set is a common way to find which ad gets engagement and conversions.
Placement and device targeting at ad set level shows ads only on **mobile, desktop, iPhone or iPad**. It can even target specific device models.
Combined with interest targeting, the message gets very specific.
Example: a Star Wars phone case, shown only to people with the matching phone model who like Star Wars.

Hyper-stacked targeting produced huge numbers of ad sets.
It needed about **50 hours per week** from three people.
Facebook ad campaigns run on Facebook and Instagram together.

So a product tested on Facebook also reaches Instagram placements by default.
In ABO test campaigns, each ad set targets **one precise interest**.

Expand the audience to the broadest set.
Then let the pixel find the buyers.

Advantage+ audience: **leave it on**.
Advantage+ audience: click **Switch to original audience**.
Conflicting instructions: Source D keeps Advantage+ audience on. Source C's ad set procedure switches to the original audience, to keep one interest per ad set.

Use Advantage+ audience **on** for broad-audience accounts.
Switch to the **original audience** when a single interest test is required.
Placements
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t:
Start on **automatic placement**.
After a few days with sales, break down results by placement.

If Facebook Feed and Instagram Feed perform best, switch from automatic to manual placement.
Then choose **only** Facebook Feed and Instagram Feed.

Keep Story ads only if they show traffic or sales.
Placements must stay on **Automatic** with Advantage+ placements on.

Choosing individual placements manually restricts delivery. Do not do it.
Use **Advantage+ placements** by default.
Switch to manual placements only when you know your audience uses specific placements.
Example: Facebook feed only, for a product aimed at people aged 50+ with knee pain.
Advantage+ placements let Meta test feeds, Instagram, Marketplace and other placements.

Then Meta moves budget to the best-performing placement after **one to two days** of data.
So you do not need to find the best placement by hand.
Manual placements restrict delivery to the placements you pick. Meta does not recommend this.

Advantage+ placement lets Meta find the best placements automatically across feeds, stories, Messenger and Reels.
Leave placements on **Automatic** (at ad set level).
Automatic placements: Meta distributes one ad across all placements. You do not build separate ad sets per placement.

Meta moves budget to the placement where return is highest.
It pulls budget back when that return drops.
Meta placements include: Facebook desktop and mobile news feed, the right-hand column, Facebook Stories, Instagram Stories, Audience Network (ads on partner apps and websites), Marketplace,

Messenger and WhatsApp.
Ad previews list where the ad can appear: Feeds, In-stream ads for reels, Stories, Status, Reels, Apps and sites, and Facebook Search results.

Advantage+ placements chooses these automatically.
So the preview is the quickest check of where the warm-up ad will be shown.
Leave placements on **Advantage+ placements**.
Schedule and start time
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: **Do not restrict** Facebook ads to certain hours. Facebook (run by Meta) learns the best times within about **1-2 days**.
In slow hours, when few people buy, Facebook spends very little, about **$1**.
**Launch** Facebook ads about **3-4 hours** before the start time, so the review can finish. A review is Meta's check of the ad before it runs.
The start time is set at the ad set level. An ad set is a group of ads that share one audience and one budget.

Ad delivery can be scheduled around the hours when sales come in. Delivery means when and how often your ad is shown.
The seller's best hours were **12 AM to 6 AM and 4 PM to 12 AM**.
Automatic rules paused ads during the midday hours.
**Set the start date** to the next day at **12:00 AM** in the ad account time zone. The ad account is the Meta account that holds your ads.

A midnight start spreads the budget over all 24 hours.
Other start times can leave the ad set unspent for hours, then spend the whole budget in **one hour**.

Starting late in the evening, for example at 10 pm or 11 pm, makes spending abrupt.
The budget can be used up within **two to three hours**.
Set the start date to **the next day at midnight** so Meta can pace the budget across the day. Pacing means spreading spend evenly over time.

Set the start date and time to **12am** in your local time on the next day. This is the start setting for new test ad sets.
Schedule the start for **midnight**, local time, on the following day.
Ad set > Schedule: **leave the start date empty** to launch when Meta approves the ad. The ">" means "then": go to Ad set, then Schedule.
To launch at a set time, such as midnight on a sale day, enter that start date and time in the Start date field.
Scheduled start and end times use the time zone of the **ad account**. They do not use your time zone or the website's time zone.

When the ad account and the website are in different time zones, **convert the times**. Convert means changing the clock time to the other zone. Do this so the ad starts when the website change goes live.
Ad set > Schedule > End date: set an end date for **time-limited sales**. Example: a sale from Saturday midnight to Tuesday midnight.

**Leave the end date off** for evergreen campaigns. Evergreen means they run all the time.
Budget scheduling: **leave it untouched**.
Keep the A/B test **off** until you set one up on purpose. An A/B test compares two versions of something.
The seller's best-hour practice is one case. The rule against hour limits applies to standard setups.
Advantage+ Settings
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: Advantage+ is Meta's automatic mode. It makes more choices for you.
**Turn off** the Advantage+ sales campaign recommendations at CBO campaign level.
CBO (Campaign Budget Optimization) means one budget sits at campaign level, and Meta shares it across the ad sets.
Advantage+ campaign budget: **turn on** for CBO. Enter the budget at campaign level.
Advantage+ audience: **leave on** for broad audiences. A broad audience is a wide group with few limits.

Advantage+ placements: **keep on**. Placements are the spots where the ad appears, such as the feed or stories.
Advantage+ placements: **use by default**.

Advantage+ placement is set at **ad set level**, in the ad set procedure.
Advantage+ campaigns: **one ad set**, several ads, and the budget on the ad set.
Advantage+ sales campaign toggle: **shown on** in the recommended setup. A toggle is an on/off switch.
Advantage+ campaigns scale with the same strategy as other campaigns. Scale means increasing spend when results are good.
Show more settings contains Budget scheduling, A/B test, Audience segment reporting and Special ad categories.
**Leave Budget scheduling untouched.** Keep the A/B test off until you set one up on purpose.
**Only declare a special ad category** if the ads are political, employment or finance related. This is rare.
Learning Phase
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: Meta's **learning phase** is the start period where the algorithm tests your ad. The algorithm is Meta's automatic system that picks who sees the ad.
The algorithm tests the ad's creative against audiences. Creative means the ad's images, video and text.
It shifts delivery toward people who engage. Engage means click, watch or react.
Choosing a **purchase** conversion goal gives fewer events than choosing add to cart. A conversion is a sale or other goal action you track. An event is one recorded action.
But purchase events are more useful for a dropshipping business. Dropshipping means you sell products without holding stock, and a supplier ships them.
Start Facebook ads at a minimum of **$50 per day**.
Lower daily budgets do not gather enough learnings to leave the learning phase. Learnings means the data Meta collects.

So **scaling takes longer** with low budgets.
**Optimize for conversions only after about 30 conversions.** Optimize means aim the ads at that goal.

Below that, **optimize for clicks**.
New creatives in a scaling CBO may receive **little or no spend**, so they cannot be judged.
Under CBO, after about **a week**, the campaign shifts most budget to the best interest ad set. Interest means a topic people care about.
Learning-phase guidance for a new pixel: **ABO** keeps spending under control. ABO (Ad set Budget Optimization) means you set the budget for each ad set yourself.
A pixel is a small code on your website that reports visits and sales to Meta. A new pixel has no purchase data for Meta to optimize with.
Ad level is the single ad, at the bottom of the structure: campaign, then ad set, then ad.
p.h: Ad level: identity, creative, destination and previews

p.t: Ad > Identity > **Facebook Page**: choose the page the ad runs from. A Facebook Page is your brand's public page.
If an Instagram account is linked to the page, **Meta selects it automatically**.

Threads can be connected, or the Instagram account can be used for it. Threads is Meta's text app.
Branding can be ignored.

**Do not connect** an Instagram account to the Facebook ad.
If a viewer taps the brand name and finds a neglected Instagram profile with few followers, the brand may look like a scam.
Ad level: identity, creative, destination and previews (continued)
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: Without the connection, **clicks go straight to the landing page**. A landing page is the page a visitor reaches after clicking.
Ad > Ad setup > Create ad with **Manual upload**: upload your own image or video files from the computer.
"Products from your catalog" is for showing catalog products. A catalog is your product list from the store.
"Use existing post" is for **boosting** a post that already exists. Boost means paying to show a post to more people.

Ad > Destination: enter the **website URL** people go to after clicking. URL means web address.
Use a collection page or a product page.

**Leave the phone number empty** for call options, unless calls are wanted.
Ad > Destination > Use shop: keep it **Default off**.

Shop checkout is an extra step that keeps people on the platform.
Checkouts happen on the website anyway.
Ad > Creative > Source URL: **leave empty**.
Meta can pull promo codes, email signup offers and site links from the website. This is usually not needed. A promo code is a discount code.
Ad > Creative > Product catalog: **turn off** the catalog section if the catalog is not fully optimized. Optimized means set up well and complete.
Catalog products should only show below the ad when the catalog is optimized.
Ads Manager autosaves each change. Ads Manager is Meta's screen for building and managing ads.

It shows **"All edits saved"** or "Verifying your edits" at the bottom of the screen.
**Wait for the saved message** before leaving the page, so the last change is not lost.
Draft campaigns and ads **always show at the top** of Ads Manager, no matter which campaign is selected. A draft is an unfinished or unpublished item.

They do not mean the account is wrong. They can make the list hard to read.
Ads Manager shows a campaign score next to new campaigns.

A **score of 100**, with the note that the recommended setup is in use, means the settings match Meta's suggested setup.
It is a setup check, not a measure of performance.
Creative count and copy units
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: Copy means the written text of an ad.
For each creative (each image or video), use **3 primary texts**, 3 headlines and 1 description. The primary text is the main text above the ad.
Fill in the primary text, headline, description and the **call to action button** (Shop now). The call to action button is the button text people press.
Meta Ads Manager is used to create and manage the campaign, ad set and ad levels.
Start with the **recommended setup**, not an improvised one.
Meta's Power Five framework is a named set of rules. Its first rule: **apply the recommendations first**. Then change only where they fail to produce profit.
Stay on the **recommended structure** for a first launch.
Keep the campaign on the **default settings** that Meta recommends. Default means the setting you get when you start. Change a setting only where a test calls for it.

Audience: Meta's learning is driven by the pixel's purchase data.
Placements and schedule: let Meta optimize with **automatic defaults**.

Budget per ad set: **$50 per ad set** for a single product with three creatives.
**$10-15 per ad set** for initial product tests.

**$15 per ad set**.
**$5 per ad set** for a new-store ABO test.
**$1 a day** is the minimum to keep a campaign active.

**$50 a day** is the minimum for learning.
Use the **higher budgets** for multi-creative tests. Use the lower budgets for tests of one interest at a time on ABO.
CBO versus ABO: **CBO is the default** for beginners, mid-stage accounts and scaling. Mid-stage means accounts that already have some sales.

**ABO is recommended** for testing new interests, new stores and creative tests.
One source advises against ABO entirely.

Switching direction: **move from ABO to CBO** after purchase data.
**Switch to ABO** after real purchase data.
Switch from CBO to ABO after **around 80-100 purchases**.
Where the sources disagree (continued)
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: Read these as different phases. CBO to ABO happens after the CBO has rich data, for cost-cap control. A cost cap is a limit on what you pay per sale.

ABO to CBO happens once Meta can use the purchase data for allocation. Allocation means how the budget is split.
Number of testing CBOs: **two separate CBOs** for the test.

**Up to two** testing CBOs in parallel. Parallel means running at the same time.
**Three CBO campaigns** in parallel.

A main CBO plus **CBO 1 and CBO 2**.
Keep **at most two** testing CBOs in parallel and no more than three in total.

Campaign count: **one CBO with one broad campaign**.
**2-5 campaigns** as Meta's guidance.
A **seven-campaign** account structure.

A **single product per campaign**.
Use **one campaign per product**. For multi-product, use one campaign per product.
Keep the account structure small.

Ad sets per test: **6-10 interest ad sets**.
**7-8** ad sets.
**5** ad sets.
**4 per CBO**.

**4 duplicates** to make five.
Use **5 ad sets** for a single-interest test with 15 ads.
Creatives per ad set: **3**.
**3-5** creatives per ad set.

**At least 3** creatives per ad set.
**2-3 minimum** in CBO.
Age: **usually 21 and above**.
**18 to 65+**.
**25+** for a Swiss German test.

Start time: **midnight local time or 12:00 AM**.
One source picked **6:00 a.m.** as its own choice. 12 p.m. or 12 a.m. also worked.

Hour restrictions: **do not restrict hours**.
The seller's best hours were **12 AM to 6 AM and 4 PM to 12 AM**.

Campaign-level audience: keep **one broad campaign** with no interest tests.
**Test one interest per ad set** in ABO.
Advantage+ audience: **leave on**.

Switch to the original audience to keep **one interest per ad set**.
Placements: **Automatic or Advantage+** placements as the default.
**Manual placements** only when data shows a specific placement wins.

Conversion objective: **Purchase** for every test. An objective is the goal you pick for a campaign.
**Clicks** while below 30 conversions.
Account structure and objectives
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: The Sales objective is the setting for Advantage+ shopping campaigns.
Select **Sales**, then **Advantage+ shopping campaign**.
For cold traffic (people who do not know your brand yet) selling products on Facebook, **conversion campaigns** are the usual objective. A conversion campaign aims for sales.
**Retargeting** is often run as a traffic campaign. Retargeting means showing ads to people who visited before. A traffic campaign aims for visits.
The reason: conversion campaigns need a steady number of conversions in a set period before the algorithm optimizes well.
Advantage+ shopping campaign is Meta's automatic sales campaign type.
Use Advantage+ shopping campaigns only with **more than 400 purchases** over the last couple of months.
Include the existing-customer setting in account settings once the account has solid sales. This setting covers people who already bought.
Advantage+ shopping campaigns require a minimum budget of **at least $50**.

They are based on the account's own purchase and engagement history (pixel data).
They use **broad targeting**.

Fields are the boxes you fill in.
Conversion location: **website**. Use website and shop only if Shop is enabled.
Countries: select the **top 5 countries** by performance.
Custom audience: add a custom purchase audience of the **last 180 days** when the account has enough sales. A custom audience is a list of people you pick from your data.

Budget and start: set a minimum budget of **$50** and a start time of the next day at midnight.
Ads: add **at least 3 to 5** of the best-performing ads.
Setting up an Advantage+ campaign from a proven campaign, which is a campaign that already made sales:

1. **Choose** the campaign that is performing best with your strongest ads.
2. **Duplicate** that campaign. Duplicate means make a copy.
3. When Facebook offers a manual setup or Advantage+, **select Advantage+**. Manual setup means you choose every setting yourself.

4. Set **only the country, age and gender** targeting. Targeting means choosing who sees the ad.
5. **Leave all other targeting decisions** to Facebook.
CBO and ABO: choosing the budget level
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: Use **CBO** when it works for the account. Meta then shifts budget to the best-performing audience pocket.

A pocket is a small slice of the audience.
If CBO does not perform, **ABO is the fallback**. A fallback is the backup choice.

Campaign-level budgets **hand control to the algorithm**.
Ad-set budgets **keep control with the advertiser**. The advertiser is you, the seller.

Use **ABO when testing**, because it gives control over spend per ad set.
CBO works when the account already has winning audiences and winning creatives.
CBO may fade after about **a week**. Fade means results drop off.
Architecture means how your campaigns are built and arranged.
A product-testing ABO campaign with **five ad sets at 8 GBP** daily budget each (UK) gives a total daily spend of **40 GBP**.

GBP means British pounds.
The campaign-level daily spending limit must also be **at least that amount**. Otherwise it will cap spend. A cap is a maximum.
If you run creative testing as a CBO campaign to spend more, set a minimum ad spend per ad set of **3 to 5 USD**.
This forces Meta to spend roughly evenly on each ad, so **every creative gets enough data**.
When testing with a CBO campaign on a budget of about **$50 to $100 per day**,
p.h: CBO audience test on a small budget

p.t:
set a minimum spend per ad set of roughly $15 to $20.
This ensures each audience gets enough spend to show its performance.
It stops **one audience** from taking the whole budget before the others are tested.
The goal of this test is to find winning audiences and creatives, **not to be profitable yet**.
Which minimum applies: for **creative tests**, use 3 to 5 USD per ad set.
For **audience tests** with a CBO budget of about $50 to $100 per day, use roughly $15 to $20 per ad set.
Pockets and audience splitting
p.s: Campaign structure: CBO, ABO, objectives and budget setup

p.t: In a CBO (Advantage campaign budget) or ABO setup, a **pocket** is the slice of an ad set's audience the platform is

delivering to right now.
The algorithm moves spend toward the pockets that **perform best** on a given day.
For this reason, **one broad audience** can be split across several ad sets to reach different pockets.
To change the launch date of several ad sets at once, **click the first ad set**, hold Shift and click the last ad set.
p.h: Editing launch dates and budgets in CBO

p.t:
Then edit the date.
The change applies to all of them.
**Leave ad-set budgets empty**, because the budget is set at campaign level.

The ad algorithm **keeps optimizing** in the background.
Changing campaigns too early **resets** that optimization.
**Let a campaign finish learning** before judging or editing it.
For a traffic retargeting test, set Settings > Campaign > Campaign Budget Optimization to **Off**.
Campaign Spend Limit is optional. It was left unset in this setup. A spend limit is a cap on total spend.
Set Settings > Ad set > Optimization for ad delivery to **Link clicks**. This is the goal Meta aims for.
Other options exist: Landing page views, Impressions or Unique daily reach. Impressions means how many times the ad is shown. Unique daily reach means how many different people see it each day.
Link clicks is the setting used here.
Set Settings > Ad set > Dynamic creative and offers: **leave dynamic creative off**. Dynamic creative means Meta mixes parts of the ad by itself.

**Do not add an offer** for standard static retargeting. Static means the ad does not change.
An offer, such as a coupon (a discount code), can be tested later in an irresistible offer ad.
Set Settings > Ad set > Schedule: for ordinary retargeting, **run continuously** from the start date.
For a time-limited campaign, such as a Black Friday offer (the big sale day after Thanksgiving), **use a start and end date** that matches the promotion length.
